children: *U.S. Seeks to Phase Out Russian Uranium Ahead of Full-Ban on Imports
*U.S. Move to Expand Use of Nuclear Energy Will Require New Sources of Uranium
U.S. Uranium Conversion in Focus as Russian Import Ban Looms — Analysis
By Anthony Harrup

The U.S. bid to expand use of nuclear energy to meet rising electricity demand has the country facing a challenge to reduce its dependence on foreign uranium supply with a ban on Russian imports due to take full effect at the end of next year.
The U.S. has the world's largest fleet of commercial nuclear reactors with 94, and relies heavily on imports for the uranium used to fuel them, from mining to conversion and enrichment.

Enrichment requires separating heavier uranium-238 atoms from the lighter uranium-235 atoms needed to create the chain reaction that releases energy. To do that, the uranium is first converted into a gas and then spun at high speeds in centrifuges.
The gas is made by mixing uranium with hydrofluoric acid and fluorine to make uranium hexafluoride, or UF6, in a process known as conversion.

"Conversion is a massive bottleneck," said Christina England-Livengood, a partner in White & Case's project development and finance practice. "It's such a critical piece that's missing in the supply chain."
The only company in the U.S. that is doing uranium conversion is Solstice Advanced Materials at a facility in Metropolis, Ill.

The Metropolis Works plant was idled in 2017 as the shutdown of nuclear facilities in Japan, Germany, and elsewhere in the wake of the 2011 Fukushima nuclear accident lowered demand and helped depress the conversion market.
"It became more economical to procure uranium conversion services than it was to produce," said Jeff Dormo, senior vice president and general manager of refrigerants & applied solutions at Solstice.

But with nuclear energy undergoing a revival, Solstice restarted the plant in 2023 and has invested more than $100 million to raise production.  The plant restarted with capacity of about 7,000 metric tons a year, and "we are now at a point where we have line of sight for 10,000 tons annual production," Dormo said.
The 2024 U.S. ban on enriched uranium imports from Russia is scheduled to go into full effect in 2028, when current waivers are due to expire.
Solstice, which markets its UF6 through ConverDyn, a 50-50 joint-venture with General Atomics, aims to help by supplying U.S. enrichers with UF6.

"Our expansion and the debottlenecking that we have done thus far goes a long way to making sure that we are in a good position domestically to have supply for some of the historical Russian supply that was coming in," said Dormo.

In 2025, the U.S.'s main sources of uranium were Canada, Kazakhstan, Australia and Uzbekistan, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. Russia was the top supplier of enriched uranium accounting for 26% of enrichment services, ahead of France, the U.K. and the Netherlands, according to the EIA.

"The Russia issue as it relates specifically to the U.S. is more about enrichment capacity and, to a lesser extent, conversion," said Jacob White, ETF products director at global asset management firm Sprott, which runs the world's biggest physical uranium trust.

Domestic supply is unlikely to be enough by 2028, and utilities will likely rely more on allied suppliers and inventories. But as fuel represents a relatively small share of a nuclear plant's overall costs, the effect of higher uranium prices on power costs should be manageable, he added.
"Uranium supply is a real longer-term challenge that will require substantial investment, but it will not topple the nuclear industry's tremendous momentum," White said.
The Trump administration has a stated goal of quadrupling U.S. nuclear energy by 2050, and last year ordered a streamlining of regulations to speed up the effort.
The Nuclear Regulatory Commission is proposing new rules aimed at making the permitting process more flexible and adaptable to new technologies.

The idea is that developers would have to demonstrate why their projects are safe rather than meeting prescriptive safety rules, said Tison Campbell, a partner in K&L Gates' energy, infrastructure and resources practice.
"It's less work up front for the regulator," he said. And while it seeks to remove some perceived regulatory barriers, "it could involve a lot more effort on the part of the industry," he said.

Although there are currently no new large-scale nuclear plants under construction in the U.S., even the existing reactors will need to find alternative sources of enriched uranium during the next two years, said Pavel Molchanov, investment strategy analyst at Raymond James.
"Longer term there will be more domestic processing in the U.S. Will that be enough by 2028? The jury is still out on that," Molchanov said.
